claims.text: Conventionally cast Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 forms several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
The primary phases in conventionally cast Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 arise under slow or moderate cooling.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
Melt spinning Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 at a cooling rate of at least 10^6 K/s will suppress extensive primary crystallization.
Cooling at at least 10^6 K/s will increase amorphous-phase retention relative to conventional casting.
Cooling at at least 10^6 K/s will enhance thermal stability during subsequent reheating.
Ultra-rapid cooling kinetically limits nucleation and restricts atomic diffusion during solidification.
Kinetically limited nucleation and restricted diffusion inhibit the formation and growth of primary crystalline phases.
Inhibition of primary-phase formation produces a predominantly amorphous microstructure.
At ultra-high cooling rates, atomic mobility becomes too low for crystallite nucleation before the liquid is quenched into a glassy state.
Rapid freezing minimizes heterogeneous nucleation sites.
Controlled reheating below the DSC-measured crystallization onset temperature permits structural relaxation without full crystallization.
Melt-spun samples will have a significantly higher amorphous fraction than conventionally cooled samples.
Melt-spun samples will have a higher glass-transition temperature than conventionally cooled samples.
Melt-spun samples will exhibit a wider supercooled-liquid region than conventionally cooled samples.
Melt-spun samples will exhibit delayed exothermic crystallization events during reheating.
Conventional cooling rates below approximately 10^5 K/s yield extensive primary crystallization in this alloy.
Cooling rates below 10^6 K/s are insufficient to suppress crystallization in this alloy.
Rapid quenching generally favors amorphous-phase retention in metallic glasses.
